paragraphs.text: OF PAMPHILUS. PSALM 119. A Song of Ascents. Those who have fallen away from the good things of God climb back up to them once they have prepared themselves for the ascent. Having shown that preparation fully in the first psalm, the Psalmist now introduces the ascent that comes through afflictions. "From a deceitful tongue." That is, from every false belief and deception. Someone at the beginning of his progress needs to be kept from being led astray by plausible arguments. "What shall be given to you?" and so on. The Word hears the one who has prayed, in keeping with "While you are still speaking, behold, I am here," and answers him, saying: "Take courage, friend. You know that you have a powerful protector and champion, who takes up arms on your behalf against your enemies. He has sharpened arrows against them and prepared desolating coals for them, and he will pursue them with punishments. What more, then, do you ask to be given to you? Or what do you want added to you, after the Mighty One has made such great preparation against the ungodly?" "With the tents of Kedar." Kedar can mean "frost of a generation" [?] and "darkening." So he says: I have dwelt with the tents of darkness, that is, of the body of death; and my soul itself, he says, has long been a sojourner many times over. ¹ Isa. 58:9. [Ke]dar is interpreted as "darkening" [?].

"I lifted up my eyes to the mountains." The one who has been set free from slavery under his enemies, and is already on the very road that leads to the city of God, lifts his eyes up toward the mountains, this way and that. He considers and searches for where his help will come from. But after looking around at every part of the world and at the heights, he finds what he seeks in none of the things perceived by the senses. Then, rising with his mind and the eyes of his soul to the Maker and Creator of all things, he comes to rest there and sings the second song, saying: "My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." "The Lord will guard you." The sleepless God himself guards the one who always looks to God, and he shelters that person's right hand, since he does right deeds and drives off his enemies with his own right hand. It is above all the right hand of those dear to God that the enemies try to plot against. So it is said: "And Joshua was clothed in filthy garments, and the devil stood at his right hand." — Above all, God guards a person from evil, even if he allows outward things or the body to suffer. Concerning Job he gave the command: "Only preserve his soul." The soul needs guarding at the time of its departure from life and at its entry into the city of God. What good is it if someone falls halfway along the road and perishes? Therefore call no one blessed before his end. "The sun shall not burn you by day." A bright cloud does not allow those who journey according to God to be scorched by the sun, and in the same way it helps them so that they suffer no harm from the light of night either.

PSALM 121. "I was glad because of those who said to me," and so on. As he walks the road that leads to God and is taught about where it ends, he is filled with gladness at the mere hearing of the things to come. That is why he acknowledges that he has found good and excellent teachers in those who said to him, "Let us go to the house of the Lord." He hurries on all the more, making the journey with gladness. — Most of those returning from Babylon were a young people, born there as Babylonians. A few among them, however, were old men of great age, who had gone down there from Jerusalem and stayed through the seventy years, after which they came back together with the young people. When the young people asked these elders where they were travelling, they answered [?], saying, "Let us go to the house of the Lord." When the young people heard this, they were glad— (Two manuscripts read "Savior." Perhaps read "seventy-year." Ed.)

"These things we bring you as good news. We also carry in our memory, accurately, the way the city was built, its very pattern, so to speak, and its shape. It was not a city scattered here and there, nor split up and divided into many parts. It was so built that it seemed to be a single house, because of how closely and harmoniously its buildings were joined together." That is why it is said: "Like a city whose fellowship is joined together in one." In their minds, all the souls that are with God are like this, as are the living stones from which the true temple of God has been built, fitted together in the same mind and the same purpose. "For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, as a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord." There he commanded them to sacrifice, to pray and to hold their festivals, so that they would not wander everywhere and find an excuse to go off after idols. He called this God's testimony, because it was the greatest proof of his providence. There the law was read, along with accounts of ancient achievements, and the people gathered together, binding their love for one another fast. "Ask, then, for what makes for the peace of Jerusalem." For always, he says, remembering you continually, O Jerusalem, we talk about your peace with our brothers and our neighbors, that is, with the young people, and by teaching them about you we lead them to long for you. And all our prayer was offered for the sake of the house of our God, as we sought good things from God for you.

PSALM 122. "To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven." Since heaven is God's throne, he is said to dwell in heaven. But no one who stores up treasure on earth could say to God, "To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven," for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The eyes of the fool are on the ends of the earth, or on whatever he desires; at times he looks at a woman in order to desire her. But the eyes of the righteous are always turned toward God. "Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters"

The young people, having heard the good news from the elders through the song before this one, say: I hope in nothing else but in you, who dwell not in the earthly Jerusalem but in heaven. Only those who have been freed from captivity and are strong in the soul's power of insight can fittingly say this. The eye of the soul benefits when it looks upward, and is harmed when it looks downward.

PSALM 123. "When men rose up against us." Those who said, "Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us," now give thanks to God because they have been heard. The person of insight, who keeps God before his eyes, is taught to say these present words. So Israel offers a song of victory to God, the giver of victory. The elders teach the

[young?], and the disciples obey. It is fitting [?] for Israel, who has God within himself, to say: "If it had not been that the Lord was among us." Such was the Israel led by Moses, to whom it was said, "Be silent and hear, O Israel," and "The Lord will fight for you, and you shall keep silent." "Then they would have swallowed us alive." The time of distress, however violent, is short-lived, like a torrent. "Blessed be the Lord," and so on. Whom should we bless and praise for not being caught by the men who wanted to swallow us alive, if not the Lord who is among us? Those who rushed to hunt us down so that they might devour us were eager to [?]. Savage as fierce lions, they longed to hunt us with their teeth. But they did not get what they were so eager for, because the Lord did not give us up. We bless him for rescuing us from the murderous men set against us.

PSALM 124. "Mountains are round about her." These words are spoken by those who returned to the visible Jerusalem after their long [exile?], as people now in safety. Their confidence rests not in the place but in their trust in the Lord, [since?] it is now better [?] to dwell in Jerusalem. And since this [?], in what respect was the people better [?]? Of the place it is said that mountains are round about it; but of the people, on whose account the place too has been honored, [it is said that] God, who also guards the place, [is round about them?] when they are worthy [?]. "[The Lord will lead them away?] with those who work [iniquity]"

PSALM 125. "When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion." It is prophesied that the apostles will say these words about themselves and about those among the Gentiles, and will afterwards answer concerning sowing and reaping. In David's time there was no captivity, so perhaps he says these things about the spiritual captivity. Someone else will say that the future is being revealed prophetically. — A part of the captivity, having returned from Babylon and recovered Jerusalem, sends up the present song with good hopes for those who were left behind in Babylon. They say that our joy has not yet been completely fulfilled; that will happen when the whole nation returns from the enemy's land to its own. The rendering of the other translators supports this sense. Where we read "we became like those comforted," they all agree in saying "we became like dreamers," not seeing our free- [editorial fragment: "...or 'at these things' ... and the sense requires ..." [?]]

-dom when awake, but only imagining it. Our joy will be real, both waking and dreaming, when the rest of our brothers also return from captivity. Then the nations too will call us blessed for having recovered our own members, for the body of those who are being saved is one. "Then our mouth was filled with joy." Those who speak of divine things bear the fruit of the Spirit, which is joy for those who hear them. Their mouth is filled with joy and their tongue with exultation, and from them joy and exultation flow. When this happens, those of the nations who are being taught say, "The Lord has done great things for them." And speaking of themselves, they give thanks and say, "The Lord has done great things for us; we have become glad." By the rivers of Babylon we sat down and wept; but when the Lord turned back the captivity, our mouth was filled with joy. When we set a guard over our mouth, and [fulfill] "The mouth of the righteous meditates on wisdom," and "Open your mouth, says God," and similar sayings such as "Our mouth is opened to you, Corinthians," then we shall truly say, "Then our mouth was filled with joy." And a little further on: When we guard our ways so as not to sin, then our tongue will be filled with exultation. Philip's mouth too was filled with joy when he opened his mouth and, beginning from "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter," proclaimed the good news of Jesus to the Ethiopian eunuch. "The Lord has done great things for us." Above, the two verses were spoken as though the return from captivity were already taking place. Now the Prophet says these things as one still in captivity. The first, I think, is a prophecy about the apostles; the second is spoken in the person of the nations. The words from "The Lord has done great things for us" to "like torrents in the south" belong to those among the nations. "Turn back our captivity, O Lord." They fittingly added these words to the earlier ones. We do not say this, he says, because we are blind to the kindness already shown to us. We acknowledge that God has done great things for us and that we have already come into gladness. Yet even so, we pray and plead for our members who are left behind: "Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like torrents in the south." It would be absurd for those who lack the knowledge of God to marvel at the kindness shown to us, while we who have received godliness suffered from ingratitude. "Those who sow in tears," and so on. Whoever sows in tears sows to the Spirit, as one of those who are called blessed for their tears. And whoever already laughs in the spirit reaps eternal life with exultation. — To those who ask about the remaining captives, the Divine replies: "Blessed are those who weep,

for they shall laugh." If those in Babylon do this, sowing good hopes through their weeping, they will reap exultation. In place of the tears they shed when they were led away [?], they will receive the joy of the return. And though at that time they preserved only a small seed of godliness, they cultivated their own souls there and will bring back much fruit when they return. Up to the seventh song, the things concerning the captives of the circumcision were foretold. PSALM 126. According to the Hebrew and all the translators, the present song is by Solomon (just as various psalms bear the names of various authors). He spoke it prophetically when he was building the temple. The Jews were proud of how strong the building was, and foreseeing by the divine Spirit the [?] ... is foretold.

those who fear the Lord. In line with this, then, you will understand who is called blessed in the present song: all those who fear the Lord. But better, and higher than those who fear the Lord, is the one who has come into perfect love, for "perfect love casts out fear." Those who fear will walk in many ways. Perhaps the one who loves walks in one way, the One who said, "I am the way," in whom the many ways also end, as in a harbor. And he rightly said, "Blessed are all." Whether slave or master, whether maimed in body, whatever one's condition, none of these things stands in the way of this blessedness of which he speaks. The blessedness people give one another is unsafe and easily overturned. It is made up of words alone and swamped by countless troubles. The one who fears God is not like this. Freed from these waves, he sits in calm and in harbor, gathering the fruit of true blessedness. "You shall eat the labors of your fruits." The other translators rendered "the toil of your hands." They speak as of a farmer who enjoys the crop he has worked for. So it is with one who strives along the road of godliness, storing up food for himself for the life to come, in proportion to the labors he has put in. Virtue and labor according to God are food and joy for the soul. Such is the one who fears the Lord. But the one who loves, being already perfect, will eat the heavenly bread, according to the saying, "Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of heaven." "Your wife shall be like a flourishing vine." Even taken literally, these things are given to the one who fears the Lord as to someone not yet perfect, and not to the one who loves him with all his soul, with all his heart and with all his strength, for "Eye has not seen," and so on. To the one who fears the Lord a wife is given, of whom it is said, "A good wife is a good portion," and "A valiant wife, who can find?" Such a woman is more precious than costly jewels. In the same way, a wicked wife would be wrath from God. "Your sons like young olive shoots." So too sons are given by God to the one who fears the Lord. They are not like most sons, but are like young olive shoots that surround and crown his table. If someone says that those who do not fear the Lord often have plenty of sons and a thriving wife, we shall reply that the present blessing does not simply promise a wife and children. It promises this whole picture: a wife likened to a vine, and children likened to young olive shoots. Such are not the [wives and children] of the ungodly. ... bearing [fruit] beyond the others, are given to the one who fears the Lord. [This is clear] from the perfect man who says, "But I am like a fruitful olive tree," and so on. For the produce of such an [olive tree?] is said to be like young olive shoots

"The righteous Lord has cut through the necks of sinners. For all the wicked who persecuted will perish wretchedly." — The righteous Lord breaks the neck that people do not bow beneath his kindly yoke. But he does this with a kindly purpose, so that they may cast off their vigor and strength for wickedness and submit to the Lord, before whom all things are naked and laid bare. Where we read "cut through the necks of sinners," Aquila rendered "cut down the nooses of the ungodly," Symmachus "cut down the nooses of the lawless," and the fifth edition "the collars of the lawless." The passage refers to the snares the ungodly have prepared in their plots against the righteous. Through these words Scripture also foretells the final end and the destruction of those who, in every age, attempt to make war on the Church of God and his people

PSALM 129 [?]. The saying "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" cannot be applied to the people of Christ. Unlike the first people, this people cried out from the depths, since it shares in the Spirit, which, according to Paul, searches all things, even the depths of God. In ordinary speech, too, "deep" is a word of praise, as in "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" And he says to Ezekiel, "I am not sending you to a people of deep lips and heavy tongue." But the people who are deep in understanding, the same people who spoke the song before this one, intercede with groanings too deep for words and cry out to God from their hearts, not with their lips. So it was with Moses, to whom it was said, though he was silent, "Why do you cry out to me?" The present prayer belongs to one who asks for what he ought, and who readily offers himself for what he asks [?]. Bearing witness to this above all, he said in the preceding song: "Often have they fought against me, yet they could not prevail against me." These are the ones who will also say, "For your name's sake I have waited for you, O Lord." Attentive ears are spoken of because the one power of God both hears and sees. By "cry" he means not the loudness of the voice but the disposition of the will. "If you should mark iniquities, O Lord." Not everyone in the Church can say, "Often have they fought against me, yet they could not prevail against me." So he sends up the present plea on behalf of the weaker ones, who cannot endure persecution. Or perhaps the same person says these things about his own iniquities before his calling. "With him is plentiful redemption." He gave his precious blood as a ransom for us, having become the Lamb of God, for he bears our sins and suffers for us. He has also wrought redemption for his people, as Zechariah says; and, as the holy Virgin says, "He has helped

So this song and the one before it fittingly contain words of humility spoken by one made perfect in the Lord, especially one who can say, "For your name's sake I have waited for you, O Lord." David, it seems, had learned from the words of the Holy Spirit that there is propitiation with God, and plentiful redemption with him if one believes. So he necessarily presents himself to the Redeemer. That is why the psalm is headed "Of David," as a plea to turn away faults [?], in which he lists his own good deeds. Never, he says, was I lifted up like a ruler over his nation. Nor did I grow puffed up by looking away from God and slackening my firm stand in his fear. Nor again did I spend my life in rich luxury. Nor did I think more highly of myself than what I actually possessed, as do those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight. "Let Israel hope in the Lord." Just as I, says King David, great as I was and such a man as I was, made myself humble and brought myself to the propitiation, to the Redeemer and Savior, so I urge the rest of Israel to come to the propitiation with confidence. I know for certain that he will redeem Israel from all its iniquities, if it runs to him.

PSALM 131. "The Lord swore truth to David." David had sworn an oath, and God swore one in return to him when he sought to learn the place. God granted him the gift that [the Lord] would come forth from him, "so that through two unchangeable things," as Paul says, "in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong encouragement" about the things he prayed for. "Of the fruit of your body I will set upon your

Since you, he says, prayed to know such things with such faith, wishing to learn the place where the Savior would come among men, receive the promise yourself as well, and become a servant of the saving birth. For the fruit that is to come will be yours, coming forth from your line and from your seed. Therefore the throne will be given to him as promised, because no one else is worthy of the throne promised to you but the one who will come forth from you. So Gabriel says to Mary: "And God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever." "If your sons keep my covenant." His disciples and successors will sit on it, that is, on the throne of Christ. Yet nothing is grudged to your sons either, O David, that is, to those of the circumcision, if they accept Christ and keep my covenant and my testimonies. These are not the ones given through the first lawgiving, but the ones I will teach them, which are later to be handed down to them through the new covenant. For if

…should keep these things, they too will sit upon your throne, which has been prepared for Christ. “Her provision I will richly bless; her poor I will satisfy with bread.” In the anagogical sense, the catch of Zion is those who, like fish, are caught alive every day in the nets of the gospel and the apostles. Her poor are the blessed ones, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven, and they feed on the bread that came down from heaven. Her priests too, having first clothed themselves with righteousness, as he said, are clothed by God with salvation. Then he speaks of the holy ones, those who stand out in the Church for their virtue and way of life. Of them Aquila said, “With praise they shall praise,” and Symmachus, “Speaking well, well-” [?]

“But upon him my sanctuary shall flourish.” He says this about John, in keeping with what the Lord said: “He was the lamp that burned and shone.” These words can also be read another way, with reference to the times of persecution. Symmachus said, “his sanctification”; for the sanctuary of our Saviour in the Church sanctifies the whole inhabited world.

PSALM 132. “Behold, what is good or what is pleasant, but for brothers to dwell together,” etc. Not everything good is also pleasant, nor is what is pleasant always good. Many things are sweet but base, just as others are laborious but good. But the concord and peace of souls that share one mind and one belief are praised for having both at once, the pleasant and the good. What is praised is not simply that brothers dwell, but that they are together in unity, as the Apostle says: “That you all say the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfected in the same mind and the same judgement.” The psalm teaches us not to place the good and the pleasant in the body or in the pleasure of the flesh. “Like the dew of Hermon, which comes down upon the mountains of Zion.” Hermon is a mountain next to Lebanon, on which much snow collects, and the Word has called this snow dew. That dew is gathered from many drops and is formed and frozen into a single body. So he fittingly used it to picture the concord and harmony of the Church, though through a further image: not the snow that stays on Mount Hermon, but the snow that comes down upon the mountains of Zion. Mount Hermon was brought in so that we might grasp how much snow there is. But to show the harmony of the commonwealth that lives according to God, he said that it comes down upon the mountains of Zion.
“For there the Lord commanded the blessing.” “There,” he says, among the brothers who dwell together in unity; and life, not ordinary life, but immortal life.

PSALM 133. “May the Lord bless you from Zion.” It had already been said to Abraham, “Those who bless you [?]”; and in effect the one who does this blesses himself. If this holds for Abraham, how much more for the Lord! For he has no need of our blessing. Rather, each of us does himself a favour and blesses himself, and is blessed in return by the Maker of all things. That is why it first says, “Bless the Lord,” and then, “May the Lord bless you.”

PSALM 134. This song of praise has the same words as the last of the Songs, so it is fittingly placed beside it. That is why “Alleluia” is written at its head: “allelu” means “praise” and “ia” means “the Lord.” One might say that the opening lines are a hymn which, like a prelude, rouses those who are commanded to praise God, and who begin their praise with “O Lord, your name endures for ever.” The psalm instructs its hearers, turning them away from idols, and teaches the knowledge of God. Those who were now coming from the nations needed exhortation of this kind. He also calls them servants, since they had not yet received the Spirit of adoption. Before the washing of regeneration, such people have a place in the house of God, in its forecourts, but have not reached the innermost parts; they have been introduced, but not perfected. There are different courts, because the lives of those being introduced also differ. It is a mark of progress, after praising the name of the Lord, to praise the Lord himself. For one must first learn that there is a Word of God who presides over the whole world and is its master, and then learn about his essence and power and come to know the only-begotten Son of God. “Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good,” etc. Because the Lord is good, praise him. The reason for praising him is that he is good not by participation, but in the same way as the Father. We praise him not only in words but by sharing in his good things. And since we must act in a way that befits contemplation and the works described in theology, “Sing to his name” has been added, for this is sweet and better than any kindness. We praise him because he chose for himself Jacob, who supplants passions and vices, and made him chosen for having put an end to the wrestlings that arise from vice and passions. He also chose as his own possession the one who came after him, Jacob shown forth through progress as Israel. That is why he is a people of possession, having become special out of all the nations, [?] concerning essence and existence, by sharing in the One who is, the wise and [?]. “All that the Lord willed he did in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the deeps.” All the things the Lord made are good, since

they came into being by the will of God. But if there is anything in heaven, such as the spiritual forces of wickedness, or on earth, such as sinful men, or in the seas, such as the wickedness of the dragon, or in the deeps, such as the wickedness of the evil beings who are ordered to depart there, God did not make it by his will. For evils will not come forth from the mouth of the Lord, and the [?]

“Who brings forth winds out of his treasuries.” The words “out of treasuries” do not mean that there are actual treasuries of winds. They show how readily the one who commands is obeyed, and how easily creation stands prepared. Someone who keeps things in a treasury brings everything out freely and whenever he likes; in the same way the Creator of all things made everything with ease and handed it over to nature. “Who struck the firstborn of Egypt.” Some say that only universal and heavenly things are governed by God's providence. So he shows that human affairs also concern God, who both punishes the ungodly now and claims the race of the godly as his own. In former times the portion of the Lord, that is, of God the Word, was his people Jacob, and Israel was the allotted share of his inheritance. But since that people fell away through the ungodliness it committed, it was said to him after he became man: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” “O Lord, your name endures for ever.” Nothing is so much the work of divine Providence as teaching people that the universe is not without a master. That is why his remembrance has been established among us for all time. His servants learned his greatness through what came before, and so they are taught to say these words and are encouraged. They have learned that they will be comforted, since judgement follows for the rest of the people, those who have recognised his name and keep his memory; and over these, as over servants who need pardon, he is moved to compassion. “The idols of the nations are silver and gold.” He has finished speaking of the Lord as God and has listed the mighty works of his providence. Now, still addressing as servants those who have just come out of polytheistic error, he sets beside this the refutation of the gods they used to worship. This follows from what he said above: “For I know that the Lord is great, and our Lord is above all gods.” Our Lord did this and that, both in universal matters and in particular ones; but the gods of the nations, which you too once believed in through error, were nothing but dead and dumb idols. Symmachus put it gracefully. In place of “May those who make them become like them,” he translated, “May those who make them become as they are, and everyone who trusts in them.” For those who devote themselves to lifeless things as gods truly have souls turned to stone. They suffer the same fate as the things they worship: they have eyes but do not see, and ears but do not hear.

“May those who make them become like them.” The people just mentioned will become, or have already become, like their own gods. But to those who have been taken into God's lot and are called his people he says, “Bless the Lord,” that is, acclaim him, and so do yourselves great good. First the people of God is called to bless, the one called the house of Israel, the lower rank of the multitude. Second, rising higher in rank, comes the house of Aaron, and third the whole priestly tribe, called the house of Levi. Above them all are those who fear the Lord. These were the ones to whom the whole hymn was addressed, those called servants at the beginning of the psalm, namely those who come to the faith from the nations. The whole Jewish nation is covered by the three ranks just named: Israel, the house of Aaron, and the house of Levi. Who else besides them could those who fear the Lord be, except those who have come from the nations to the word of God? They too are taught to bless: “Blessed be the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem,” that is, in the ever-abiding city of God, in which the true dwelling place of God might be understood (10).

PSALM 135. “To him who alone did great wonders.” This is wonderful even taken literally. Heaven, by sight alone, shows the wisdom of God through its size, its beauty and its long endurance. The earth is washed by waters on every side and yet keeps its own stability. To all these things the psalmist joined God's everlasting mercy, because God made everything not out of any need of his own but purely out of love for humankind. “To him who struck Egypt.” He says: if you are not convinced that the whole world and its parts are governed by God's providence and power, and you suspect that he may overlook particular and human affairs, know that he cares for things on earth no less than for things in heaven. From time to time he punishes people who are extremely godless and impious, as he once punished the Egyptians and the land of Egypt itself. He also protects and fights for those dear to God, and not only for them but also for their descendants. So it was with those who were then freed through Moses from slavery among the Egyptians. The God who is over all freed them himself, with nothing other than an outstretched hand and a mighty arm. This would be the (9) [Ed. note: “of” is missing.] These things, he says, are for those who make idols; but let the people of the Lord and his lot enjoy acclaiming him. First comes the house of Israel, the lower rank; then the one rising higher, the house of Aaron; then the whole tribe of the priests, the house of Levi; [?] then the whole tribe of the priests, the house of Levi; and above all, those who fear the Lord. To them the whole hymn was addressed, and earlier they were called servants, by which he meant those from the nations who have believed. For who are those who fear the Lord, besides the three ranks of the Jews? And by Zion he means (10) [Ed. note: “to show”; perhaps read “shows.”]

[?] Word (11), through whom the love for humankind of the all-good God has worked its benefits toward people, both of old and now. “Sihon, king of the Amorites.” The name Amorites is interpreted as “embittering talkers,” and the name of their king Sihon as “temptation and provocation.” Those who are clever at sophistical deceit are embittering talkers. They want all who love the truth to be talked into deception and enchanted, and their aim is to tempt and provoke. Bashan is interpreted as “shame” and signifies the vice that brings shame on the wicked. Its king Og is killed together with Sihon. So the land passes to Israel. They had held it wrongly, busying themselves sophistically and with a depraved disposition over the nature of things, and thought they ruled it. But the land, understood in this interpreted sense, is taken from them and given to Israel as a possession to inherit, since Israel is a true servant of the Cause of all things. “For in our humiliation the Lord remembered us.”

In the passages above it was shown in various ways that Israel is not the race of the Jews but a particular manner of godliness (12). “For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel”; nor, as the Apostle says, is true circumcision that which is outward in the flesh. “He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, not by the letter but by the Spirit; his praise is not from men but from God.” So he also redeemed us who are from the nations from our enemies, and did so more fully than he redeemed them; for we are the circumcision and the true Israel. Those who came out of Egypt escaped bodily tyrants, but they carried their impious ways with them in their souls, and they fell in the desert after turning to idolatry. Us, however, he truly redeemed from the enemies of our soul, and in our humiliation he remembered us more than them. They were slaves to the Egyptians in their bodies, but we were the playthings of demons in our very souls and were brought low under the evil spirits. So great is God's mercy that he not only cares for the godly and looks after those who draw near to him, but provides for absolutely everything on earth, irrational creatures as well as rational ones. He supplies food to every living creature on earth and gives each kind what suits it and what it needs to live; and from there his care reaches up again to heaven. That is why the text, after saying, “Who gives food to all flesh,” sends us back up to heaven, saying again: “Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy endures for ever.”

…to the Hebrews, and its heading does not say whose it is or what kind of psalm it is. It is a bare prophecy, spoken in the person of those who were in Babylon. Note this too: in some copies of the Seventy its heading reads, “Of Haggai and [?]”

“Blessed is he who will repay you your recompense [?].” The blessing will rest on those who repay Babylon in kind, and on the one who dashes her infants against the rock and destroys them. And truly, the first blessing would have been never to have seen Babylon at all and never to have been caught up in the confusion of its evils. But if someone has once found himself there, having fallen from better things, he would be blessed if he did to them what he had suffered, took the Babylonians captive in his turn, and led the very souls of the Babylonians over to the fear of God. And if he did not let their infants grow up but crushed them against the rock, he would be more blessed than many. You would not be wrong to say that the infants of Babylon are the seeds of vice and the beginnings of the sins that bring confusion. The one called blessed here will be eager to destroy them by the saving word (for the rock was Christ), so that they do not grow and do not go on to become deeds.

PSALM 137. “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart.” The perfect man loves God with his whole soul, power and strength. He does not divide the powers of his love among other things but is wholly attached to God alone. In the same way, the psalmist gives thanks to God with his whole heart. He is confident in this freedom of speech. He knows that in the great theatre of human life the divine angels and ministers of God are watching and observing his progress in God. So he renders to God the worship that is due and says: “And before the angels I will sing to you.” “I will worship toward your holy temple.” He promises to worship toward a holy temple, meaning the Church, or the heavenly Jerusalem, of which the temple on earth was a type. Then he gives thanks [?] for the mercy and truth of God. Here Symmachus has “for your mercy and your truth.” For having received God's mercy, he has been set free from types and symbols and has been found worthy to worship God in spirit and in truth. “Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, O Lord.” We have often observed that the psalms whose heading names neither a hymn, nor a song, nor a psalm, nor anything else have a different character from these. The present [?] shares in the force [?]. For David, having given thanks for what came before, says: “But I am not the only one among kings to have been found worthy of this; there will be very many such.” That is, [?] the proclamation of the Saviour; and especially when the

full number of the Gentiles has come in and the Saviour's second coming takes place. For then the glory of the Lord will be seen to be great. Following a certain Hebrew usage, future events are sometimes expressed by commands and wishes. He prophesies about the knowledge of God that was to spread to all nations. “For there will be a time,” he says, “when all the kings of the earth will give thanks to you and will hear all the words of the mouth of God, and they will sing in the ways of the Lord.” These things were fulfilled at no other time than after the gospel proclamation of our Saviour. The ways are the virtues, which lead to the knowledge of God. “The Lord is high, and he looks upon the lowly.” David learned what was spoken in him and through him by the prophetic Spirit. So he is confident that God looks upon the lowly and fights at his side in his afflictions. “If I walk in the midst of affliction, you will keep me alive,” etc. Symmachus said it more clearly: “If I walk through the midst of affliction, you will keep me safe; against the fury of my enemies you will stretch out your hand, and your right hand will save me.” “The Lord will accomplish”

PSALM 138. “O Lord, you have tested me and known me.” The time of our life also has certain measured intervals fixed by God. So he says: you yourself have searched out all the time of my life and the road I have travelled. “Your knowledge has become too wonderful for me.” He says: the knowledge of these things exceeds my power and lies beyond my understanding, so that I can neither discover nor express them. Whatever I may say is small and slight compared with the divine power, whose comprehension escapes my littleness and nothingness. “Your eyes saw my unformed being.” He says: what I have not yet done you see as already accomplished, and those not yet born you know as already born. “Unformed” can be understood in two ways: as innocent and free of malice, and as not yet examined in me. For the [?] ought to be called the work; and an unformed soul is one that has not yet been shaped by virtue and knowledge. “Men of blood, turn away from me.” “They will take your cities in vain.” He had said, “But your friends, O God, have been greatly honoured by me.” So he fittingly rejects God's enemies and drives them away from himself. He also remembers that a time will come when God himself will slay the sinners, so he already drives them far from himself. In this way he will not become their partner or, by being near them, share in the harm they do. And since they take your cities in vain for contentious arguments and quarrels (the divine Scriptures are called cities, and the heterodox take them up

in vain and not as they should (13)), I turn away and shun them. “Test me, O God.” At the beginning he said, “O Lord, you have tested me and known me.” Now, as if he had not yet been tested, he says, “Test me, O Lord, and know my heart.” Earlier it was said, “You have searched out my path and my lot, and foreseen all my ways”; but now, “Examine me and know my paths.” Perhaps, then, he is not contradicting himself. Earlier he simply said that he had been tested and known; now he prays to be tested so that his heart may be known. To be pure and upright in heart is greater than simply to be pure and upright. Likewise, to be tested so that one's heart is known goes beyond simply being known as one who has been tested. And it is greater to have one's paths known after examination than to have one's ways foreseen. That is why he added, “And see whether you have seen lawlessness in me,” that is, in my habits and disposition. Another reading has, “And see whether there is a way of lawlessness in me”; that is, consider whether lawlessness ever travelled through my soul, so that traces of its [?] remain in me. Nevertheless, [?] such sinlessness has been achieved for me from you and through you; at any rate you have guided me on the [?] way that leads to immortality and incorruption.

PSALM 139. “Coals of fire will fall upon them.” For a man with such a disease will be punished by his own doing. “Evils will hunt down the unjust man to destruction.” What does “to destruction” mean? Many are hunted for salvation, like those caught by the apostles and by holy men. But the wicked, when they are hunted by vice, are hunted to destruction as well. For every unjust man, ruined by his own vice as by a disease of his own, will suffer the punishment he deserves. Vice is enough, in place of any other punishment, [to ?] the soul that has it

Solomon learned from this, his father's teaching, and says in Ecclesiastes: “The end of the matter; hear it all: God will bring every deed into judgement, along with everything overlooked, whether good or evil.” He says that even now God will judge, avenging the poor and needy man who is now oppressed. After this he brought the psalm to a happy end. Its heading is “For the end,” and it speaks of the hope stored up for the righteous. Symmachus has “in your presence.” What could be better than to see God face to face with a purified mind, as in the Saviour's beatitude: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”? Those who attain this will give thanks. Patrologia Graeca XXIV.

This psalm, too, has a title in keeping with the preceding one. It is David's, and it has the same force of prayer. But it has something more: it is more doctrinal, and from its very opening it teaches more, and more useful, things. It says: "I cried." We should not at all suppose that he used a loud voice and shouting, for God hears even those who are silent. So, too, Moses is said to have been told: "Why do you cry out to me?" Rather, the one who possesses great doctrines about God, asking something of God with surpassing disposition and faith, cried out to him in this way. That is why he also says with confidence: Since I am such a one, and cry out such things, "attend to my voice when I cry out to you," as one who has pure not only his mind but also the [?]

[?] To these he fittingly added: "The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice." You will understand this from the Apostle's saying: "I want the men to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or quarrelling." For he, too, mentioned at once what belongs to the mind and what belongs to action. But the ungodly never lift up their hands. That is why it was said to them: "Whenever you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my face away from you." One must lift one's actions on high and perform them in a way pleasing to God. "Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness." Do not allow my mind, once and for all firmly established, to be turned aside and bent toward the opposite. Instead of "to make excuses for sins," Symmachus rendered "to think lawless thoughts," interpreting the sense of the passage more clearly. Then he passes again to the practical, saying: "with men who work lawlessness, and I will not join with their chosen ones." Here again Symmachus interpreted more clearly, saying: "With men who work injustice, may I not even eat their delicacies." For I shall not be with them, he says, if you, Lord, set a guard on my mouth and preserve the treasure that was stored up for me beforehand. Their "chosen ones" would be those who allege excuses for the wicked things they do. Worse still are those who act lawlessly without excuse and without any concealment. "Their judges were swallowed up near the rock." Symmachus has: "For my prayer is still within their evils; their judges will be plucked away by the hands of the rock; they will hear my most sweet words; as when a farmer breaks up the earth, so have your bones been scattered beside Hades." Now he gives the reason for not joining with sinners. For fellowship with them, he says, is enough to scatter my soul, and within their evils [?]

[?] they see their own rulers and judges dragged down [?], as though plucked out by a solid [?] power. "Do not take away my soul." Instead of "do not take away," Symmachus has "do not empty out"; that is, do not allow the good treasure stored up in me to be emptied out. For then I shall depart without fear, he says, when sinners fall into their own nets.

PSALM 141. "Of understanding, of David, when he was in the cave; a prayer." Psalm 56 has a similar title, as follows: "For the end; Do not destroy; of David, for an inscription on a pillar, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave." The story is found in Kingdoms: "And David went up from there and stayed in the strongholds of Engedi. And when Saul returned from pursuing the foreigners, they told him, saying, 'Look, David is in the wilderness of Engedi.' And Saul took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to seek David and the men with him, facing the hunting ground of the deer. And they came to the sheepfolds by the road, where the cave was. And Saul went into the cave to relieve himself, while David and his men were sitting in the inner parts of the cave." Such is the story of Saul and the cave. As we have often said, the name David is interpreted in different ways and taken in different senses. When you find it applied to the person of the Lord, it is interpreted "beloved"; but when it is applied to the person of those who sin and turn back, it is interpreted "despised," because of their sins. Here the name David is to be taken of the people that has sinned and come to understanding, that has shut itself up in a cave and prays earnestly with tears and makes confession, as this very title shows. The psalm likewise teaches these things. "When my spirit was failing within me." This too is said very fittingly, given the distress of the time and the place. As far as human help went, he was shut up inside the cave and cut off from every escape and flight, and not a single hope of help was left to him. Nor was there anyone to rescue his soul or to seek it out. Seeing that the spiritual enemies of his soul had brought all this about (I mean Saul's entering the cave in order to seize David), he rightly said: "They hid a snare for me." But the snare did not succeed for them, because of the prayer before us. Taking courage from the course of his life, from his deeds and
the ways in which he walked, though he was unjustly hunted and warred against, he says to God: "And you knew my paths" [?]

"To you, Lord, I cried." Here again he declares that he cries out, and not simply, but to the Lord. For otherwise he could not have uttered a sound with the enemy close by. And having declared that God was his only hope, he did not fail of his aim, for "hope does not put to shame." Indeed, he says, even if there is to be a land of the living, I declare that I have no place in it except you alone, my hope; "for you are God, my portion in the land of the living." It is as if he said: had I not had you, I would never have been counted in the land of the living. The land of the living is not the one we now tread, for this is a land of death and of the dead. It is the one which the meek will inherit, in which all the living spend their days in eternal life. "There was no one who recognized me; [?] there is no one who seeks after my soul." Someone neglected by those who are thought to preside over the churches, and not sought out at all, may fitly say this. And what follows brings in crying out to God, hoping not in leaders but in the Lord, and having a portion in the land of the living and not in a land of forgetting.

PSALM 142. Anyone who is being tested in the greatest trials and overwhelming afflictions may fittingly use the prayer before us; that is why the psalm [?] has no title. The Lord hears everyone, but he heeds few. If we heed those who make requests of us, we too shall be heeded. And the one who is confident in his own prayer calls on God to listen. Others say that the psalm is not untitled but bears the title: "A psalm of David, when his son was pursuing him." This is not found in all the translations, however. Still, what is said is not foreign to that occasion, and nothing prevents these words from being said about the persecution by Saul. "My spirit grew faint within me." The spirit of a man that is in him grows despondent whenever the heart is troubled, remembering how the enemy humbled its life to the ground and made it sit in dark places like those long dead. And my heart, he says, though troubled within me, held the suffering inside and did not break out at all, so as to come into the open before everyone and make known to those outside the [?]

"I remembered the days of old." Moses, too, commands: "Remember the days of old"; and David says again: "And I remembered the years of old, and meditated." So it is fitting that one troubled in heart, treating his own ailment, should run back to his former days, the ones before the trouble, in which he did well, or else to the ancient histories. And having taken up this memory, he meditates on the works of God and on the works of his hands, and he finds no small consolation in the ancient

Scriptures. He learns from them that God visited the people of old after countless afflictions and trials, and how many cures and benefits he gave them. And by meditating on the principles of creation, too, he was healed in soul, being taught that human life is not without providence, and that the soul of one who is troubled is not beyond healing. The Word of God watches over all and stands over all, healing the brokenhearted. "I spread out my hands to you; my soul is like a waterless land before you." Having remembered the days of old by studying the divine Scriptures, I spread out my hands, showing you my deeds made pure through repentance. So I thirst for you, O God, and for the healing that comes from you, not only as a deer thirsts for springs of water, but as waterless, dry land longs for the rain that comes down on it. And if my soul is like a waterless land, it is such in relation to you, God. In itself, and compared with other people, it is fertile and flourishing with good fruits; but before you it is waterless in this sense, that "no one living will be justified before you." "Hear me quickly," and so on. "Do not turn your face away from me." In pressing times of hardship, whether in persecutions or in the most extreme dangers, when someone's soul is in peril, the spirit within it failing and the heart within it troubled, those who pray for the things of Christ should say, as David did: "Hear me, Lord." But there is no need to use these words for merely human affairs. As long as your face deems me worthy of what is its own, your light is in me and all my darkness has been driven away, so that I can say: "The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord." But if you should ever turn your face away from me, I come to be in darkness, the darkness in which all are who go down into the pit. And in that pit there is nothing other than what is called the outer darkness. "Let me hear your mercy in the morning." In trials we need divine mercy. This would come about if we devoted ourselves watchfully to prayer, especially at the morning hour, so as to be able to say: "O God, my God, to you [?]"

[?] From lying on the ground, I have lifted up my soul to you. Show me the way of repentance, or the way that leads, together with release from the body, to heavenly things. For how could a mortal understand the ways of [?]? Perhaps someone who has walked the earlier ways, Moses and the prophets (as it says, "Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord"), and who after these seeks the good way, will say to its Father, who knows

the way of the sons: "Make known to me the way in which I should walk." At the Father's assent, this way reveals itself and says to the worthy: "I am the way; for no one comes to the Father except through [me]."

"For your name's sake, Lord." This is like: "Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory." For we must not trust in ourselves. But let the one who has nobly endured trials hope to obtain these things, as one who has walked the narrow and hard way. "In your righteousness you will bring my soul out of affliction." It is truly an affliction of the soul to have one's life humbled to the ground and to sit in darkness. And whoever is troubled in soul by base thoughts and the burning of the passions is afflicted, too. No one else frees [?] from such affliction except God, who knows the secrets of the heart. Someone whose soul is troubled by the harassment of deceivers would also be greatly afflicted, especially when he cannot refute their sophisms and fears that he may fall away from the truth. But God brings the soul out of every such affliction, shining on it and flooding it with his own radiance and leading it to live according to his righteousness, as was just shown. By God's mercy the enemies will be destroyed. They will not perish in their substance, for that is impossible, but they will cast off the disposition that makes them enemies of the righteous man and afflicters of his soul. In this way the righteous man will be at ease, living in peace without war. Appealing to the one he entreats to grant his request, he added: "For I am your servant." The greatest of possessions and boasts is to be called God's servant. The Saviour, too, shows how great this is when he says to those with him: "You call me Lord and Teacher, and you say well, for so I am." Nothing drives away our enemies so well as spiritual contemplation.

PSALM 143. If you refer these words to David, especially since in some copies the psalm is titled "Against Goliath," you will say that they suit him. According to the history, he conquered that man not with ordinary armour but with trust in God. Claiming God as his teacher, on that occasion he brought Goliath down with a stone from his sling, and at other times he killed the wild beasts of the field, strangling them with his hands. It was especially fitting for him to say these things while playing the psaltery, when, using his hands and fingers instead of a plectrum, he drove away the invisible demons that were troubling Saul. But if the words are applied to every righteous person, you will say that all the deeds of one who loves God bring about the overthrow of the opposing powers, God being the teacher of this stretching out of the hands. And by his fingers he signified activities down to the [?]

smallest matters of human life. Moses, too, routed Amalek by stretching out his hands. But consider whether it is not Christ who speaks, having routed the invisible enemies. For the psalm reveals, as will be shown, his descent from heaven, the rout of the demons, the calling of the nations, and the two peoples. "Who subjects my people under me." It is God's work to subject his own people to human leaders. Unless this came from God, it would never happen. Moses would not have led so great a multitude if the Lord had not subjected his own people to him, not by weapons or human battle lines but by a higher power. "Lord, what is man, that you made yourself known to him?" The text asks, as a question, what man is, wishing to teach us that man is something great. Otherwise he would not have been able to receive the knowledge of God, nor would God have been so mindful of him as to send his own Word to him as Saviour and Redeemer. In the same words it also urges us to despise no human being, and teaches that no one achieves anything worthy of such a benefit. "Lord, bow your heavens and come down." Quite necessarily and consistently [he says] that the Word of God himself comes down to overthrow the enemies. For even if he does above all teach my hands and fingers how to wage war, he says, what strength does a man have, and how much power does a mortal have, one who has become like vanity, to be able to stand against so great an army? Therefore you yourself, O Lord, bow the heavens and come down. By "heavens" he means the powers conceived of in him. And he condescends as a father does to infants, and as a teacher to his disciples. "Send forth your hand from on high." Send forth, the psalm says, the hand that makes and preserves all things, to deliver me and rescue me out of many waters and from the hands of foreign sons. Being rescued from many waters may be taken to mean being rescued from the wicked powers and from the devil, the king of all such powers; and being delivered from the hand of foreign sons, to mean being delivered from the people who are driven by those powers. For he called the assaults of trials and of the ungodly "waters," as he also says elsewhere: "Then the water would have swallowed us up"; and again: "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul." And consistently, after the descent of the Word of God, having seen the plot of the ungodly [?] against him, he prophesies what follows. "A new song I will sing to you." It was fitting that the new covenant, too, be mentioned in the prophecies about the descent of the Word of God; that is why it is signified by the new song. And by calling it new, he has made the first one old, as

the Apostle says. Of this song it is said: "Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth." And he also says: "Let them sing psalms on a ten-stringed psaltery," hinting at the practical life carried out through soul and body. For there are five senses of the flesh and five powers of the soul, by which the senses of the body are moved. "To him who gives salvation to kings." He who taught the kingdom of heaven makes kings of those who are deemed worthy of it, and to them he gives the salvation that comes from him, and also to those who have succeeded in not being ruled by sin. It is Christ who says in Proverbs: "By me kings reign." Knowing this, the Apostle wrote: "Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you!" Since God grants salvation to such people, the oracle fittingly sketches good hopes for David, too, as one who will be redeemed from whatever sins he ever fell into. For the descent of the Word of God has benefited David as well as the others, since he served his birth in the flesh. "Who redeems David his servant from the evil sword." The evil sword is the tongue of the godless and the words of those who devise sophisms against God in order to murder souls. The hand of foreign sons is the conduct and life of those who are strangers to godliness, whose mouth speaks vanities in myths and fictions and in errors about idols. Their right hand, that is, their more practical power, busies itself with greed and plunder. Those of the former people, too, would be of this kind, according to what has been said. From these, then, David now prays a second time to be rescued, so that he may not be caught in similar sins. "Whose sons are like young plants established in their youth."

The sons not only of the former people but of all who are strangers to godliness are like young plants established in their youth. But the flesh of the righteous man is weak, and his mind has been put to death. The daughters of those of the circumcision are adorned like harlots, "as the likeness of a temple" in which an evil spirit dwells. That is why the prophet says of them: "Because the daughters of Zion walked with outstretched necks and winking eyes," and so on. But the saints are a temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in them. The storehouses of the former overflow and spill out, for they store up treasure on earth and say: "I will pull down my barns and build bigger ones." But the treasure of the latter is in heaven. The former have prolific, multiplying sheep and fat oxen, like the abundance of Egypt; for the cattle that Pharaoh saw were fine in appearance and choice in flesh. But the flock of the righteous man consists of innocent souls and good, rational sheep.

Because the [righteous] man fears the Lord, his sons are blessed and are like young olive shoots around his table. But the sons of foreigners are like young plants established in their youth. He has no daughters, while they have daughters beautified and adorned all around like the likeness of a temple. He has sons' sons, but they do not. Further, he no longer has storehouse or barn, while their storehouses are full, overflowing from one kind of thing to another. And according to the Gospel, the birds of the air, fed by the heavenly Father, have no storehouse or barn. The sons are heretical doctrines, and their ideas are like young plants because of their novelty. The daughters are their words, beautified by their style and serving as the temple of their thought. "There is no breach in the fence," and so on. In Job, too, it is said: "Why do the ungodly live, and grow old in wealth as well?" and what follows. But he adds: "Yet the lamp of the ungodly will be put out." And in the seventy-second psalm it is said: "I was jealous of the lawless when I saw the peace of sinners," and so on. The answer to these things, too, is given in the words: "How did they come to desolation? Suddenly they perished because of their folly, like a dream when one wakes up."

PSALM 144. The words before us were not spoken on the instrument called the psaltery, nor as a song, but in another manner; the psalm is titled "Praise." "Every day I will bless you." Among the Hebrews this verse begins with beth. It teaches that we ought to render the hymn to God each day like a debt [?], and not neglect or omit a hymn to God on any day. With the mind and the thoughts and the very power of the spirit within us we exalt and bless God himself, but with our lips and mortal words we glorify God's name. I continue always to sing hymns to you, he says, and I will leave no day without its share of hymnody. Instead of "for ever and ever," Aquila rendered "still" and Symmachus "continually." Everything agrees with what came before. For having said "I will bless" and "I will exalt," he shows that our praise adds nothing to God. Rather, we bring honour on ourselves when we add praise to praise. [?] "They will exult in your righteousness." Through these words he teaches the virtues of God that reach as far as us, through which we also come to know him. For those that are above us are invisible and incomprehensible to us, and mortal nature cannot grasp them. [?] These words are the virtues of God that reach us, through which we know him.

"The Lord is compassionate and merciful," and what follows. For when we did not exist and had no being, he brought us into the light. Then, though we do many evil things and behave with contempt, he does not punish us as we deserve. [?] Instead he has mercy, and he is also patient, calling us to repentance, because he does not desire the death of the sinner so much as his repentance. And this is true not only of his own people but of absolutely everyone, since he is good to all. "And his compassions are over all his works." Because his compassions are over all his works, it follows that it is said, "Let all your works confess you." This is owed to him, so that even the things thought to be lifeless all but find a voice to give thanks and confess to the one who made them. For each of his works, fashioned in its own way, shares in his wisdom and shares, most wisely, in his creative power. But in a special and preeminent way his holy ones render the greater part of the confession. For by what they think and do they will speak of the glory of his kingdom, showing it in a foretaste, since they are soldiers who have served him and are the glory of his kingdom. And they will also tell of the power that belongs by nature to the kingdom, how each of the creatures is wholly subject to him. Those who lay claim to holiness toward you and from you are lovers of humankind, and they generously share the good things they have received with the sons of men by teaching them. For Christ is the teacher and guide only of those who have risen above human life, while those who are still sons of men have as teachers those whom Christ has taught. Paul, for example, received the gospel and was taught it not from men or through man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ, and he became a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. Indeed the Savior himself sends out the apostles to make disciples of all nations, having first taught them not to call anyone on earth teacher. What the holy ones learn from him, then, they make known to the sons of men. "The Lord is faithful in his words." God is called faithful not because he has a share in faith but because he is worthy of trust, for everything he says comes to pass, as in: "He has spoken; will he not do it, and will he not abide by it?" He also says, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." "And holy": because he gives a share of holiness to his works, just as he is also holy in those who share his holiness, and the Savior is wisdom in those who are wise according to him. "You give them their food in due season." Eusebius also says that God is not only the physician of the fallen and the healer of

the broken, but also the one who feeds all. That is why the eyes of all living creatures, rational and irrational alike, look up to him. Since all look to him with certain impulses, some natural and some learned, he, like a good father, provides food suited to the seasons, different at different times. Opening to all his creating hand, that is, his power, he generously and without hindrance fills every living thing with the enjoyment of what he gives. "The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth." Then, since only a few are able to call upon him with understanding and to be thought worthy of his hearing, he necessarily takes up the statement again and adds that he is near not to all who call upon him, but only to those who do so in truth. For he stands far off from those who are not like this, and to them he says, "Your sins stand between me and you." Of these it is also said elsewhere, "For those who remove themselves far from you shall perish." So he is near to all by his providence, but near by relationship to those who call upon him with understanding, for this is what "in truth" means. After his general providence he has added the special providence for the faithful: that he is near to such people and cares for them in greater measure. "My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name." For now I will not cease to praise God. And I pray that the prophecy may come to pass all the sooner which says, "I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh," and, "Let every breath praise the Lord." This will happen when the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, when every race of men will also be saved. By "mouth" he means the spiritual mouth, of which it is said elsewhere: all flesh will be blessing the name of the Lord, clearly "forever and to the age of the age," seeing the salvation of God and no longer being like grass.

PSALM 145. "Alleluia" means "praise of the Lord," for that is how the word is interpreted. The present psalm, then, is also a praise, which is why the text says at its beginning, "Praise the Lord, O my soul." Either the spirit is exhorting the soul, or the soul is exhorting itself. Then, obeying the command, it eagerly answers, saying, "I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I exist." If the soul is immortal, and always lives and exists, being able to do so even after its release from the body, it is saying: "So I shall never cease praising the Lord, but for long ages, through the whole course of my immortal life, I shall go on doing nothing but praising the Lord." "As long as I exist" must be understood as spoken by the soul, not as though it would cease to exist afterward, but as a promise to praise the Lord for the endless time of its existence.

This is like "It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man; it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes." He establishes this by a syllogism. "If they themselves," he says, "cannot secure salvation for themselves, what benefit could come from such people? They cannot even rescue themselves from death at the end. For the spirit of the dying man will go out wherever the one who leads it away leads it, and the rest of the man will return to his earth, fulfilling the law of nature that God laid on Adam from the beginning when he said, 'Earth you are, and to earth you shall depart.'" [?] All the schemes that he gathered within himself while he was still alive, pondering them, as though he were gathering and storing up treasure on earth for eternity, promising to do terrible things and threatening others again, will be snuffed out in a single hour, and all their thoughts will perish, that is, the thoughts of the rulers whom many admire. He could also mean the rulers of this age, for their rule too is subject to change. But the Savior alone is the cause of salvation, who says, "There is no one who saves besides me." If, then, they are saved by him and not by their own power, how will they be able to save others? "Who keeps truth forever": confirming the truth of the words he promised in the Scriptures. For he promised that at the time of judgment he would avenge those who are wronged in this present life. Another promise is: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst, for they will be filled, but you will hunger." But he also provided food in a visible way: he gave manna to the hungry in the wilderness, he fed five thousand, he fed Elijah through ravens and Daniel through the prophet Habakkuk. And he executed judgment for those who were wronged: for Joseph, wronged by the Egyptian woman, for Susanna, wronged by the judges of Israel, and for David, wronged by Saul. The divine writings are full of such things. "The Lord sets free those who are shackled; the Lord gives wisdom to the blind."

He sets free those who are shackled, giving forgiveness of sins to those bound tight by the cords of their own sins. Through these words he seems to hint at the calling of the Gentiles, the Lord's coming among men, and the healing that would come to all through it. This interpretation occurred to me when I recalled Isaiah's prophecy about our Savior, in which he says, "Behold, I have made you a covenant for the race, a light for the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out of their bonds those who are bound." So here too the Lord sets free those who are shackled. It is also said, "The Lord gives wisdom to the blind." It is wonderful how even to those who are maimed in body [he gives] more understanding [?]

"He will take up the orphan and the widow." The souls that have cast off the devil, who in wickedness had become their father and husband, are taken up as orphans and widows. When these have been taken up, the way of sinners, which is nothing other than wickedness, will be destroyed by God. These things have been said rather allegorically. By widows he means not just any widows, but those who persevere in purity and dignity; and by orphans, those who for the sake of godliness have left their parents [?]

In the present psalm, in place of "Praise the Lord," Symmachus said, "Alleluia, for a song is good," leaving untranslated the Hebrew word that means "Praise the Lord." Likewise the fifth version rendered it "Praise Yah." The psalm before this one exhorts a single soul to praise the Lord, but here "Praise the Lord" is said to multitudes. Since no one is good but one, God, it follows that everything referred to his glory and done for his honor would be good. So the psalm is good, since it is sent up as to a good God. For this Aquila translated "a good encomium," and Symmachus "a good song." Moreover, the praise sent up to God is sweeter to him than any fragrant incense and any pleasure. For truly the praise of God, sent up from a rational and pure soul, would be dear to him, and sweet if anything is, for he rejoices in and welcomes such fruit of the human mind. "Who heals the brokenhearted." Since it belongs to a savior and a physician to heal and bind up what is broken, these words may fittingly be understood of the Lord himself, our Savior, the Word of God, who said, "Those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; I came not to call the righteous but sinners." Being always a physician, he will heal from spiritual captivity those who are broken in heart and turned aside from their natural reasonings. Symmachus says, "who heals those who are crushed in heart," and [?] their wounds [?], that is, with rational bonds [?]. In this way he bound with spiritual [?] bonds the man who was wounded by robbers and crushed as he went down from Jerusalem to Jericho. "And binding up their wounds" [?]. "Who counts the multitudes of the stars," etc. [?] After healing the brokenhearted and binding up their wounds, he returns [?]

to the theme of universal Providence, showing that he cares not only for the parts of the world but also for human doctrines [?]. He alone knows the number of the stars, their positions and causes, their sizes and distances, their powers and operations, [giving] each a fitting name

"Begin to the Lord with confession." Symmachus has: "Recount confession to the Lord; make melody to our God on the lyre." Aquila: "Recount to the Lord in thanksgiving; make melody to our God on the cithara." Those who command others to confess and to sing must be different from those they command. So by these words a prophetic chorus, and an apostolic one, calls to the same God those who are not of their number, namely those from the Gentiles, saying, "Sing to our God." The text commands us to confess with the mind and the reasonings of the soul, and to sing to him with works performed through the body, as through a cithara. It customarily calls the body a psaltery and a cithara, since it is put together rhythmically and with a wise harmony. For in it the mind, striking up through virtuous deeds, sends up to God an inspired and spiritual melody. "Who gives food also to the young of the ravens that call upon him." A certain account from natural history has reached us: that ravens' chicks are not fed by their parents as the chicks of other birds are. They say that ravens' chicks are abandoned by their parents and fed by another, extraordinary power of God. Since their parents no longer come near them, they gape with their mouths for lack of food and look like creatures calling upon God, asking by a kind of natural instinct for food from the one who gave them their being. And so some food is carried from the air into their mouths, driven along by a breeze.

PSALM 147. "Who declares his word to Jacob." Eusebius also says: The present phrase, "Who declares his word to Jacob," seems to me to teach something very precise. For he did not say "who sends" or "who sent." To declare is one thing, and to send or be sent is another. The one announces and foretells what is to come; the other signifies presence, and that the one sent preaches in person. So the declaration and prediction of what was to come took place with Israel alone, but the sending would be not to Israel alone but to all the other nations as well. But perhaps someone might say: "If he did not make it known to the rest of mankind, how can he punish them, both those before the Law and those who sin everywhere in the world?" And we reply: These he judges by the natural law, the one within us, but the Israelites

by both this and the written law, so that his great kindness becomes the ground of a greater condemnation for them, since they were negligent. That is why he did not say "he did nothing for any nation," but "he did not do so." That is, he did not send them tablets or the writing on Mount Sinai; these he gave to the Jews as something over and above.

PSALM 148. In Psalm 145 the soul alone, by itself, was bidden to praise the Lord, the text saying, "Praise the Lord, O my soul." In the psalm after it, he called a multitude to praise with "Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good." In the next, Jerusalem herself was commanded to do this, in "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem." Following on from these, the present praise intensifies the injunction, enlarging the command after the partial exhortations. It urges the whole created order together at once, both visible and invisible, to the praise of God. At the beginning it calls on the things in the heavens and in the heights; then it proceeds to the things on earth and in the deeps. This is not because all these share in soul and reason; rather, it bids those who do share in reason to look at these things and, learning the wisdom that went into them, to sing hymns to their Maker. "And all deeps." Another interpreter said that "deeps" means the region of those beneath the earth, following Paul, who said, "Do not say, 'Who will descend into the abyss?' that is, to bring Christ up from the dead"; and in Job: "Have you walked in the tracks of the abyss?" But perhaps this too signifies the mass of waters on which the Lord walked, so that "And the gates of death open to you in fear" belongs to a separate beginning [?]. "Sing to the Lord a new song," etc. Of the new song [?] sung in the Church of the holy ones, that is, of the New Testament of our Savior [?], Israel attending to the old [covenant] given through Moses [?]; but this new example [?] let it rejoice. For he himself was the Word of God who spoke with Moses and brought Israel out of Egypt, making it his own people. So he exhorts the sons of Zion first to rejoice and exult in their king. And he again was the Word of God, who was of old their king but was later rejected by them. That is why he says to the prophet Samuel, "It is not you they have despised, but me, so that I should not reign over them." But since they did not obey the call, they fittingly deprived themselves of the grace of gladness. The nations, however, recognized the king who had been proclaimed first to them

and received him. Therefore the gladness and exultation that are according to God passed over to them.
