Hence the nations throughout the whole world, in their own churches, praise the name of their king, glorifying in dance, in the chorus of the Word of God, the name of Jesus Christ. But each one also by himself [?] good works, and through the actions of the body accomplishes what contributes to the hymn and glorification of God. Fittingly anticipating this very thing, the text commands, saying, "With timbrel and psaltery let them sing to him," calling the body a timbrel and the spirit a psaltery [?], having put to death their members that are on earth and carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus. Those who exult in their king, together with [Israel], who rejoices in [the one who] made him [?], sing with timbrel and psaltery.

PSALM 149. "They will exult on their beds." In another sense, he alluded by "beds" to the death of the holy ones. For Scripture is accustomed to call death sleep, as Paul also says, "Concerning those who are asleep, I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers." And the Old Testament says, "David slept with his fathers." "The exaltations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands." Aquila strikingly presented the sense of the passage, following the Hebrew wording closely, when he said, "A sword of mouths in their hand." But of those opposed to such people it is said somewhere, "Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword"—the words of men who slay those they have captured. The text fittingly presented the sword of mouths as at work in their deeds, and the exaltations of God as in their mouth. For they used their voice to teach the word, raising up the hymn among those able to hear; and in their deeds they had power to tear down every opposing power. By their hands he means their deeds, or the work they had taken in hand. This was the word of the gospel, which was also called a sword, driving out the herds of evil and unclean spirits; and [it was given] to execute vengeance on behalf of the wronged nations and to rebuke the idolatry of the people. "To bind their kings in fetters," etc. Since there was no other way to rescue and free those long enslaved to demons than first to subdue and bind their rulers, these words are fittingly added. You will understand this also from the Savior's saying, "How can anyone enter the strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first

binds the strong man, and then he will plunder his house?" So the prayers of the apostles, their words and teachings, the life that matched them, and the deeds that worked against the demons, laid bonds on the opposing powers, especially the greater and ruling ones among them. The Savior's apostles bound the activities of these powers against the nations by their own words and their own prayers, more firmly than any manacles made of iron—binding the power by which those spirits ran about here and there—and, subduing all the nations, they brought them to their own king. "To execute among them the judgment that is written." Having received the nations into discipleship, they left behind [?] the teaching [in writing], so that they might always have it to read and keep in memory what is written. After this he very fittingly added, "This glory is for all his holy ones." For each of the holy ones gains glory through what has been handed down to us by them. Take Paul as an example, who says, "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, the authorities, and the world-rulers of this darkness." His glory also [?] are the peoples whom he freed from demonic error and brought to the word of Christ, having established the Church from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum. His glory also were his written readings, still handed down in the churches even now, in which God's judgment concerning the overthrow of the demons and the freedom of human souls is set down in writing. So it is also with Peter and John and the rest of the apostles.

Take care to notice that the first psalm of the whole book foretold the destruction of the ungodly and pronounced blessed one single person, as a rare case, who is able to escape the life of the ungodly. But the very last psalm brings every breath to the hymnody of God. Moreover, if this final word brings every breath to the hymnody of God, [it indicates] the different manner of each, with the instrument proper to each [?], giving the sound of the trumpet to the one who has risen higher [?]; for the trumpet is the loudest-sounding and requires the most power [?], to signify the apostles, whose voice went out into all the earth, for the preaching of the gospel is the loudest-sounding of all; and to those lesser than these he assigned the remaining instruments. [?] the prophetic word shows that theology must [?]: "If I speak in tongues without interpreting, but I [?]" [?] the hearer receiving the sound without understanding [?]

[?] …calls them to the singing of hymns. But since not everyone has a single way of life, nor a single disposition, it assigns [?] to each, in proportion, an instrument suited to the hymn. For one who has risen higher than all in virtue renders praise with the sound of the trumpet, since the trumpet is the loudest of all instruments, and those who use it need greater and stronger power. Such were the holy apostles of the Savior, whose sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world; for they used the mighty voice of the gospel preaching, so that people were filled with their voice. But since not everyone is able, like the apostles, to praise God with the sound of the trumpet, the word comes down to their level and bids some praise with the psaltery, others with the lyre, and others with tambourines: some through works and the actions of the body, others through the very movement of the soul, in rhythm and harmony, of the Spirit who dwells [?]… whenever he says, “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also.” And since there are three things in us [?]… the word. “Praise God in his saints.” Aquila, however, says, “in his sanctified one,” and Symmachus, “in his holy one.” “Praise him in the firmament of his power.” And perhaps this does not mean the heavens and the highest regions above them; the Holy One of God is someone else, the one of whom even the demons, struck with terror, said, “We know who you are, the Holy One of God.” Those who come to be in him will be able to send up the hymn fitting for those who have been perfected to the utmost. For what is more blessed than to be united with him, and through him with the Father? And we must also look to the prophets, apostles, and martyrs and praise their God, who granted humankind so rich a harvest of good men. “Praise him according to the abundance of his greatness.”

For each of his works calls for abundant praise, since there is no limit to his greatness. Yet he does not tell them to render a hymn equal to it, for that is impossible; rather, he asks for what is within their power, as they contemplate the abundance of his greatness.
